source_text: CAPUT NONUM, De infinitate Dei. Atque haec de primo Dei attributo, nempe absoluta exsistendi necessitate: sequitur alterum, nimirum I. Infinitas, quae hic est, summa essentiae divinae perfectio, omni termino ac limite carens. INFINITATIS vocabulum hic mutuamur ab iis, quae quantitati alias proprie tribuuntur. Dicitur autem Deus duobus modis perfectionis suae termino carere, extensive videlicet & intensive. Extensive, quia ejus natura non est praecise limitata ad unum genus perfectionum, sed in se concludit omnia perfectionum genera, quaecunque cogitari aut esse ullo modo possunt, idque in infinitum. Atque ita Deus simpliciter & absolute perfectus dicitur, quia omnis perfectio illi ita necessario inest, ut nulla prorsus illi deesse queat.
english: CHAPTER NINE. On the infinity of God.

And these things concerning the first attribute of God, namely absolute necessity of existing: there follows the second, namely I. Infinity, which here is the highest perfection of the divine essence, lacking every term and limit. The vocabulary of INFINITY we here borrow from those things which otherwise are properly attributed to quantity.

But God is said in two ways to lack a term of His perfection, namely extensively and intensively. Extensively, because His nature is not precisely limited to one genus of perfections, but in itself encloses all genera of perfections whatever can be thought or be in any way, and that infinitely. And so God is called simply and absolutely perfect, because every perfection so necessarily inheres in Him that none at all can be lacking to Him.

source_text: SEPTIMO, consensu & autoritate orthodoxae antiquitatis. Dionysius libro de divinis nominibus cap. 5: Unitas, ait, continet Deus, secundum supersubstantialem simplicem infinitatem suam. Damascenus lib. 1. orthod. fidei cap. 12: Universum, ait, id quod est, tanquam immensum quoddam & infinitum essentiae pelagus complexu suo continet. Bernhardus: Hoc Deo est esse, quod haec omnia esse. Mercurius Trismegistus Deum vocat Bonum interminatum & infinitum. Orpheus Deum appellat infinitum finem. Sic Xenophanes, Parmenides, Melissus dicunt, id quod est, nempe Deum, infinitum esse.
english: SEVENTH, by the consensus and authority of orthodox antiquity. Dionysius (On the Divine Names, chapter 5): Unity, he says, God contains according to His supersubstantial simple infinity. Damascene (Orthodox Faith 1.12): The universe, he says, that which is, as a certain immense and infinite sea of essence He contains in His embrace. Bernard: For God this is to be, which is to be all these things. Mercury Trismegistus calls God the interminable and infinite Good. Orpheus calls God the infinite end. So Xenophanes, Parmenides, Melissus say that that which is — namely God — is infinite.

source_text: QUINTO, omnem essentiae perfectionem, quae in Deo est, esse quoque intensive infinitam, hoc est, sine mensura & termino illi inesse, ita ostendo. Ens a seipso exsistens ex necessitate naturae suae, nequit esse limitatum ad certum perfectionis gradum. Atqui Deus est ens a seipso exsistens ex necessitate naturae suae, ut cap. 8. demonstratum fuit. Ergo Deus nequit esse limitatus ad certum perfectionis gradum. Atque ex hoc non tantum infinitatem Deo tribuimus absolute, sed etiam eam cum aliis attributis, praesertim affirmativis, conjungimus, ut, quando sapientiam, potentiam, bonitatem infinitam in Deo esse dicimus.
english: FIFTH, that every perfection of essence which is in God is also intensively infinite — that is, inheres in Him without measure and term — I show thus. A being existing from itself by the necessity of its nature cannot be limited to a certain grade of perfection. But God is a being existing from itself by the necessity of its nature, as was demonstrated in chapter 8. Therefore God cannot be limited to a certain grade of perfection.
And from this we attribute infinity to God not only absolutely, but also join it with other attributes, especially affirmative ones, as when we say infinite wisdom, power, and goodness are in God.

source_text: Formale consistit in negatione termini, qui est, tum quaelibet entis perfectio, cum praecisione caeterarum perfectionum, tum quilibet perfectionis gradus, cum praecisione reliquorum graduum. Haec vero proprietas ita Deo convenit, ut in nulla creaturarum inveniatur, quia omnis creatura necessario certum definitumque perfectionum numerum, earumque omnium definitum ac limitatum gradum a Deo omnis perfectionis fonte capit.
english: The formal consists in the negation of a term, which is both any perfection of a being with the precision of the other perfections, and any grade of perfection with the precision of the remaining grades. But this property so belongs to God that it is found in none of the creatures, because every creature necessarily takes from God the fountain of every perfection a certain and definite number of perfections, and of all of them a definite and limited grade.

source_text: PRIMO, sacrae Scripturae testimoniis, quae Deo magnitudinem & excellentiam supra omnes res creatas attribuunt, Job. 36.26 & 37.23; Psal. 48.2 & 95.3 & 96.4 & 97.9 & 99.2 & 145.3; Tit. 2.13 & alibi passim. SECUNDO, a summa Dei bonitate. Talis bonitas necessario est aeternis indefecta, adeoque infinita: cum omnis finita bonitas necessario deficiat a summa bonitate. Unde Gregorius Nyssenus libro de opificio hominis cap. 1. docet, Deum esse bonum, omne bonum, quod intelligendo cogitandoque comprehenditur, exsuperans, hoc est, infinitum.
english: FIRST, by the testimonies of sacred Scripture, which attribute to God greatness and excellence above all created things (Job 36:26 and 37:23; Psalm 48:2 and 95:3 and 96:4 and 97:9 and 99:2 and 145:3; Titus 2:13 and elsewhere everywhere).

SECOND, from God's highest goodness. Such goodness is necessarily undefective for eternities, and therefore infinite: since every finite goodness necessarily falls short of the highest goodness. From which Gregory of Nyssa (On the Making of Man, chapter 1) teaches that God is good, surpassing every good which is comprehended by understanding and thinking — that is, infinite.

source_text: TERTIO, Deum extensive & intensive infinitum esse ita evinco. Omni ente finito potest aliud esse perfectius & majus. Deo nihil potest esse perfectius & majus. Ergo Deus non est ens finitum. QUARTO, Deus habet omnem entis perfectionem, quia absolutum primum, unde caetera omnia dependent, necessario perfectione sua excedit reliqua omnia entia. Ergo omnem eorum perfectionem eminentiori modo in se continet, et potentia quae numquam ita exhauriri possunt ut non novas rerum species & perfectiones depromere possint.
english: THIRD, I prove that God is extensively and intensively infinite thus. For every finite being something else can be more perfect and greater. For God nothing can be more perfect and greater. Therefore God is not a finite being.

FOURTH, God has every perfection of being, because the absolute first, on which all the rest depend, necessarily exceeds all remaining beings by His perfection. Therefore He contains every perfection of theirs in Himself in a more eminent manner, and powers which can never be so exhausted that they cannot bring forth new species and perfections of things.
